scope: Selected source-linked syndrome teaching associations; clue strength is qualitative, not a validated diagnostic score.

syndromes.name: Naxos disease

clues.text: Woolly hair together with palmoplantar keratoderma
Curly hair alone

syndromes.cardiac: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, often right ventricular, with ventricular arrhythmia and sudden-death risk.
syndromes.inheritance: Classic Naxos: autosomal recessive, biallelic JUP pathogenic variants.
testing: JUP testing and phase assessment; ECG, rhythm monitoring and cardiac imaging.
gaps: Confirm the laboratory's sequence and copy-number coverage.
caveats: Hair and skin findings may precede cardiac disease. A single JUP finding does not establish Naxos; other JUP disease contexts exist.

sources.title: MedlinePlus Genetics · hair, skin and gene mapping
GeneReviews · JUP inheritance and cardiac evaluation

syndromes.mechanism: JUP encodes plakoglobin, part of the desmosomes that hold heart and skin cells together. Biallelic disease can therefore link woolly hair and keratoderma with arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

syndromes.name: Carvajal syndrome

clues.text: Woolly hair together with palmoplantar keratoderma
Curly hair alone

syndromes.cardiac: Dilated / left-predominant cardiomyopathy, heart failure and ventricular arrhythmia risk.
syndromes.inheritance: Classic Carvajal: autosomal recessive, biallelic DSP pathogenic variants.
testing: DSP testing and phase assessment; ECG, rhythm monitoring and cardiac imaging.
gaps: Confirm the laboratory's sequence and copy-number coverage.
caveats: Monoallelic DSP cardiomyopathy is a separate context and need not have this hair–skin pattern. The badge does not assign Carvajal to every DSP variant.

sources.title: MedlinePlus Genetics · Carvajal phenotype and DSP

syndromes.mechanism: DSP encodes desmoplakin, which anchors desmosomes to the cell cytoskeleton. Biallelic disease can affect skin, hair and myocardium; monoallelic DSP cardiomyopathy is a separate context.

syndromes.name: Loeys–Dietz syndrome

clues.text: Bifid uvula / cleft palate with widely spaced eyes
Pectus deformity, long fingers, translucent skin or easy bruising

syndromes.cardiac: Aortic and other arterial aneurysms, tortuosity and dissection; disease may extend beyond the aortic root.
syndromes.inheritance: These six Priority 1 genes: autosomal dominant, disease-relevant heterozygous pathogenic variants.
testing: Clinical genetics assessment, echocardiography and arterial imaging; phenotype-directed HTAD testing.
gaps: Confirm sequence and deletion/duplication coverage with the laboratory.
caveats: No single facial or palatal sign is diagnostic. Features vary across genes, ages and families; absence does not exclude LDS. Interpret the specific variant and mechanism, not the gene name alone.
syndromes.mechanism: These genes participate in TGF-beta signaling and vascular / connective-tissue biology. Disease-associated variants can link craniofacial and skeletal findings with arterial disease; manifestations differ by gene and variant.

syndromes.name: Marfan syndrome

clues.text: Ectopia lentis (lens displacement)
Long fingers / limbs with pectus deformity or scoliosis
Tall stature alone

syndromes.cardiac: Aortic root enlargement and dissection; mitral valve prolapse / regurgitation.
syndromes.inheritance: Autosomal dominant; a Marfan-associated FBN1 pathogenic variant in the appropriate clinical context.
testing: Clinical diagnostic criteria, aortic root imaging and a dilated slit-lamp examination; FBN1 / HTAD testing.
gaps: Ensure deletion/duplication analysis is available if sequence testing is unrevealing.
caveats: Ectopia lentis needs an eye examination and also has other causes. FBN1 has several allelic disorders; tall stature or an FBN1 VUS does not establish Marfan syndrome.
syndromes.mechanism: FBN1 encodes fibrillin-1, a component of connective-tissue microfibrils. Disease can involve the aortic wall, skeletal proportions and the supporting structures of the lens.

syndromes.name: Vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome

clues.text: Thin translucent skin, easy bruising and aged-appearing hands
Bruising or joint hypermobility alone

syndromes.cardiac: Arterial dissection or rupture, sometimes without a preceding aneurysm; additional bowel and uterine fragility.
syndromes.inheritance: Usually autosomal dominant; heterozygous COL3A1 pathogenic variant.
testing: COL3A1 molecular testing and specialist assessment; noninvasive arterial imaging as clinically indicated.
gaps: If suspicion persists after negative sequencing, review deletion/duplication and splice / RNA assessment with a specialist laboratory.
caveats: External signs can be subtle or absent. Generalized hypermobility alone is not a vEDS diagnosis. Fragility matters when planning invasive investigations.
syndromes.mechanism: COL3A1 encodes type III collagen. Disease-associated variants can compromise the strength of skin, arterial walls and other hollow organs.

syndromes.name: Familial hypercholesterolemia

clues.text: Tendon xanthomas, particularly Achilles or hand tendons
Premature corneal arcus
Xanthelasma alone

syndromes.cardiac: Premature coronary atherosclerosis; severe disease may involve the aortic valve / root.
syndromes.inheritance: LDLR / APOB / PCSK9: usually dominant; LDLRAP1: recessive, biallelic disease.
testing: Lipid profile, family history and clinical FH assessment; exclude secondary causes and consider sitosterolemia. Use molecular confirmation when appropriate.
gaps: Validate LDLR deletion/duplication detection; sequencing alone can miss relevant CNVs.
caveats: Xanthomas also occur in other lipid disorders and may be absent in FH. PCSK9 gain-of-function and receptor-binding-defective APOB variants matter; other variants can lower cholesterol instead.

sources.title: GeneReviews · familial hypercholesterolemia
sources.sections: Clinical characteristics; Table 1; mechanism of disease causation

syndromes.mechanism: These genes affect LDL clearance. Disease-causing mechanisms can produce cholesterol accumulation in tendons and arteries; the direction of the variant effect matters.

syndromes.name: Sitosterolemia

clues.text: Childhood tendon / tuberous xanthomas, including unusual sites
Xanthomas alone

syndromes.cardiac: Premature atherosclerosis, coronary events and possible aortic valve involvement.
syndromes.inheritance: Autosomal recessive; usually biallelic pathogenic variants in ABCG5 or ABCG8.
testing: Dedicated plasma sitosterol / campesterol analysis (GC-MS or LC-MS/MS); ABCG5 / ABCG8 testing. CBC / blood film may show hemolysis or large-platelet thrombocytopenia.
gaps: A routine lipid profile does not measure plant sterols.
caveats: Appearance overlaps FH; LDL-C alone cannot distinguish them. Diet, infant feeding, ezetimibe and bile acid resins can affect sterol results. Interpret with the laboratory and medication history.

sources.title: GeneReviews · sitosterolemia
sources.sections: Suggestive findings; plasma plant sterol measurement and false negatives

syndromes.mechanism: ABCG5 and ABCG8 form a sterol transporter. Biallelic dysfunction can impair plant-sterol elimination, linking sterol accumulation with xanthomas and vascular disease.

syndromes.name: Fabry disease

clues.text: Angiokeratomas with neuropathic pain / sweating abnormalities
Cornea verticillata
An isolated angiokeratoma

syndromes.cardiac: LVH / cardiomyopathy, conduction disease and arrhythmias; renal and cerebrovascular involvement may coexist.
syndromes.inheritance: X-linked; disease expression varies in both males and females.
testing: Alpha-galactosidase A activity plus GLA molecular testing; lyso-Gb3 is supportive. Assess renal and cardiac involvement; slit-lamp examination for corneal changes.
gaps: Normal enzyme activity does not exclude Fabry in females; molecular testing is needed.
caveats: Late-onset cardiac disease may lack skin findings. Corneal whorls can have drug-related causes. Biomarkers and a VUS alone do not establish disease.
syndromes.mechanism: GLA encodes alpha-galactosidase A. Deficiency causes glycosphingolipid accumulation in multiple tissues, linking skin, nerve, kidney and cardiac manifestations.

syndromes.name: Danon disease

clues.text: Proximal muscle weakness / motor delay with learning difficulties
Retinopathy

syndromes.cardiac: Often severe, progressive HCM in males; HCM or DCM in females. Pre-excitation, conduction disease and arrhythmias can occur.
syndromes.inheritance: X-linked, usually LAMP2 loss-of-function disease; females can be substantially affected.
testing: LAMP2 molecular testing; ECG / imaging, CK and neuromuscular, developmental and ophthalmic assessment.
caveats: There is no reliable distinctive external appearance. Weakness and learning difficulties are nonspecific; extracardiac findings may be mild or absent, especially in females. Do not exclude Danon by inspection.
syndromes.mechanism: LAMP2 supports lysosomal and autophagic function. Loss of function can produce cardiac and skeletal myopathy with additional developmental or retinal involvement.

syndromes.name: Timothy syndrome

clues.text: Cutaneous syndactyly in a child with long QT
Developmental differences or hypotonia
Syndactyly alone

syndromes.cardiac: Marked QT prolongation, ventricular arrhythmias and possible congenital heart disease / AV block.
syndromes.inheritance: Autosomal dominant, often de novo; Timothy-associated CACNA1C variants usually increase calcium current.
testing: ECG / rhythm assessment and CACNA1C molecular testing with variant-specific interpretation.
gaps: Check coverage of relevant alternative exons, including 8 / 8A; discuss suspected mosaicism with the laboratory.
caveats: Timothy syndrome can occur without syndactyly. CACNA1C also causes other cardiac and neurodevelopmental phenotypes; not every variant causes Timothy syndrome.
syndromes.mechanism: Selected CACNA1C calcium-channel variants alter channel function. Their electrical and developmental effects can connect long QT with syndactyly and other systemic findings.

syndromes.name: Andersen–Tawil syndrome

clues.text: Small mandible, low-set ears or fifth-digit clinodactyly
Periodic paralysis alongside ventricular arrhythmia
An isolated minor facial / digital feature

syndromes.cardiac: Ventricular ectopy and bidirectional / polymorphic VT; prominent U waves and prolonged QU may occur.
syndromes.inheritance: Autosomal dominant; usually KCNJ2 loss-of-function disease.
testing: ECG and ambulatory monitoring; potassium during weakness; KCNJ2 testing and specialist assessment.
gaps: Consider KCNJ2 deletion/duplication analysis if sequence testing is negative and suspicion persists.
caveats: The full triad need not be present. QU prolongation is not interchangeable with typical long QT. Other KCNJ2 mechanisms can cause different electrical phenotypes.

sources.title: GeneReviews · Andersen–Tawil syndrome
sources.sections: Suggestive findings; molecular testing; clinical description

syndromes.mechanism: KCNJ2 encodes the Kir2.1 potassium channel. Disease-associated dysfunction can affect cardiac and skeletal-muscle excitability alongside characteristic skeletal features.

syndromes.name: Jervell–Lange-Nielsen syndrome

clues.text: Congenital bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with long QT
Hearing loss alone

syndromes.cardiac: Long QT with torsades / ventricular fibrillation and sudden-death risk; severity varies, including between the two genes.
syndromes.inheritance: Autosomal recessive; biallelic loss-of-function pathogenic variants in KCNQ1 or in KCNE1.
testing: Audiology, repeated ECG / QT assessment and molecular confirmation including phase of variants in the same gene.
gaps: Review copy-number / second-allele detection if only one variant is found despite a strong phenotype.
caveats: Hearing loss is a history / audiology clue, not visible anatomy. A single variant or one variant in each gene does not establish classic JLNS. Most hearing loss has other causes.

sources.title: GeneReviews · Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome
sources.sections: Summary; establishing the diagnosis; mode of inheritance (updated 15 Oct 2026)

syndromes.mechanism: KCNQ1 and KCNE1 contribute to potassium-channel function in the heart and inner ear. Biallelic disease can link QT prolongation with congenital hearing loss.

syndromes.name: Noonan syndrome

clues.text: Facial pattern with widely spaced eyes / ptosis, webbed neck and chest deformity
Short stature or an isolated facial feature

syndromes.mechanism: These genes participate in RAS/MAPK signaling, which regulates development and growth. Disease effects depend on the gene and variant.
syndromes.cardiac: Pulmonary valve stenosis and HCM. HCM is particularly associated with RAF1 and RIT1; classic PTPN11-related Noonan more often involves pulmonary stenosis.
syndromes.inheritance: These catalog genes: autosomal dominant; disease-associated heterozygous variants.
testing: Clinical genetics assessment, ECG / echocardiography and phenotype-directed RASopathy testing.
gaps: Only three Noonan genes are represented here; this is not a complete RASopathy panel.
caveats: Features change with age. RIT1-related disease may lack short stature or pectus findings. PTPN11 variant-specific Noonan with multiple lentigines is a separate entry; a VUS does not diagnose either condition.

syndromes.name: Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines

clues.text: Multiple lentigines with Noonan-like facial / chest features
Widely spaced eyes, ptosis or short stature
Pigmented skin spots alone

syndromes.mechanism: Disease-associated PTPN11 or RAF1 variants alter growth signaling. Interpret the specific variant; the cardiac profile differs from classic PTPN11-related Noonan syndrome.
syndromes.cardiac: HCM is a central cardiac manifestation; pulmonary stenosis and conduction abnormalities can occur.
testing: Clinical genetics review, skin examination, ECG / echocardiography, hearing assessment and molecular testing.
gaps: BRAF and MAP2K1 are also associated but absent from this catalog. Confirm appropriate RASopathy panel coverage.
caveats: Lentigines often emerge during childhood and may be absent in young children. A shared gene name does not distinguish this syndrome from classic Noonan.

syndromes.name: Duchenne / Becker dystrophinopathy

clues.text: Calf enlargement with progressive proximal weakness / Gowers maneuver
Motor delay, frequent falls or difficulty running / climbing stairs
Large calves alone

syndromes.mechanism: DMD encodes dystrophin, which stabilizes muscle-cell membranes. Absent or reduced function can injure both skeletal and cardiac muscle.
syndromes.cardiac: Dilated cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias; cardiac-predominant disease can occur in males and heterozygous females.
syndromes.inheritance: X-linked; both hemizygous males and heterozygous females can have cardiac involvement.
testing: Neuromuscular assessment, CK, DMD molecular testing and cardiac evaluation.
gaps: Validated deletion/duplication analysis plus sequence assessment is essential.
caveats: Gowers maneuver and calf enlargement occur in other myopathies. Normal-looking muscle or absent weakness does not exclude DMD-related cardiomyopathy, especially in females.
